### feD’s neW roUnD of Qe faIls to IGnIte fUrtHer metals rally The us Federal reserve announced a new round of monetary stimulus on December 12th, committing to buy $45 billion per month in longer-term Treasuries on top of the $40 billion per month already in place to purchase mortgage-backed bonds. The Fed also indicated that interest rates would remain near zero until unemployment falls to at least 6.5%. a caveat to this was that inflation should not exceed 2.5% and that inflation expectations are contained. however, the new measures were simply replacing the expiring “operation Twist” programme, whereby the Fed bought an identical amount of Treasuries but paid for them with the proceeds from sales and redemptions of short-term debt. The new purchases will be funded with an expansion of its $2.8 trillion balance sheet. Given the latest us unemployment rate of 7.7%, this suggests there will be some time to go before the Fed will need to think about raising rates, and indeed its own forecasts suggest a timeline stretching into late 2015. although the Fed extended the monthly amount of its Qe programme, market action suggested that this was already built into expectations as prices failed to react. in fact, metals prices turned downwards subsequently as the increasing likelihood that the us would drop off the “fiscal cliff”

loomed large. another dampener was the Fed’s downgrade to its us economic outlook, seeing GDP growth of between 2.3-3.0% in 2013, down from 2.5-3.0% in september. The wider market is even more pessimistic. adding to this is continued uncertainty over european debt and the region’s economic growth prospects over the coming year. Despite the trials and tribulations faced by the global economy this year, we are currently in a position where metals markets seem to have largely shrugged this off; at least if we judge them by price performance. of the lme base metals, the star performer through December 13th was tin, which gained 19.7% for the year-to-date. This was followed by the two “ugly sisters” of lead and zinc, which gained 12.8% and 12.0%, respectively. in zinc’s case, this has been in spite of the poor fundamentals and rising stocks faced by the metal. copper was next up, adding 5.8%; perhaps its enhanced macro credentials hampered its upside potential relative to some of its other smaller, less liquid, counterparts? aluminium, which continues to be dogged by ever-increasing global (and particularly chinese) output and record high lme inventories, was the second-worst performer on the complex, but still gained 4.8%. Nickel was the stand-out; its fundamentals have certainly not been outstanding by any means, as production has outpaced consumption (especially as the stainless steel market has remained weak), but it was the only base metal to record a price fall for the year-to-date. The metal’s price fell 5.7% through December 13th. average prices for base metals for the year-to-date, with only a couple of weeks of trading left, are: $7,951 for copper (on a cash basis) – we currently forecast average 2013 prices of $8,190/tonne; $2,016/tonne for aluminium – forecast for 2013 of $2,020/tonne; Nickel $17,532/tonne – forecast of $18,710/tonne; Zinc $1,942/tonne – forecast of $2,080/tonne; lead $2,050/tonne – forecast of $2,265/ tonne; Tin $20,992/tonne – forecast of $23,965/tonne. ###### Base meTals & oTher commoDiTy Prices ###### Base meTal Prices iN major curreNcies 300

##### EConoMiC inDiCatoRs revised oecD leading indicators show that the overall composite index has remained stable at 100.2 since july. The overall indicator for the eurozone slid to 99.3 in october, from 99.4 in the previous month, whilst the measure for japan was unchanged at 100.2. more positively, the us indicator rose to 100.9, from 100.8 in september. elsewhere, the chinese indicator picked up to 99.6 after holding at 99.5 over april-september, while that for india also rose, to 97.3, stemming the downtrend seen over prior months. The eurozone economy shrank for the second consecutive quarter in the three months to september, constrained by weak government spending and business investment. reflecting ongoing weakness, industrial output slid 1.4% month-on-month in october, the second consecutive month of decline, which included a 2.6% decline in Germany. in annual terms, eu iP contracted by 3.6%, after shrinking by a revised 2.8% in september. more positively, more recent data showed that the business and consumer confidence index rose for the first time in nine months in November to 85.7, from a three-year low of 84.3 in october, whilst the manufacturing Pmi rose for the second consecutive month in December to 46.3, from 46.2 in November. however, the Pmi remained in contractionary territory and, despite the recent upturn in some indicators, we remain cautious about the extent and sustainability of any recovery given weak underlying activity and high unemployment, amongst other factors. meanwhile, in japan, conditions remain downbeat. The japanese economy shrank by an annualised 3.5% in the third quarter, as falling exports (weakness in europe was a major factor) and the territorial dispute with china restricted capital expenditure, whilst the conclusion of some government subsidies dented consumer spending. although industrial production did improve 1.8%

month-on-month in october, it was down 4.3% yearon-year. Furthermore, and more recently, consumer confidence continued to slide to 39.0 in November, from 39.8 in october. The Tankan survey also reflected the deterioration in sentiment; the headline diffusion index for large manufacturers fell from -3 in the september quarter to -12 in the final quarter. meanwhile, the manufacturing Pmi fell to a 19-month low of 46.5 in November, from 46.9 in the previous month. in the united states, GDP growth improved in the third quarter, rising 2.7% on an annualised basis, up from 1.3% in the june quarter. since then, trends in key indicators have been somewhat skewed by the disruption caused by hurricane sandy; iP rebounded 1.1% in November, following a revised 0.7% drop in october. meanwhile, the ism manufacturing Pmi in November registered a surprise fall, to 49.5 from 51.7 in october. more positively, November us consumer confidence rose for the third consecutive month to 73.7 from 73.1 in october, buoyed by the improvements in job growth over recent months. Finally, the latest data have supported our expectations for a fourth quarter rebound in the chinese economy. industrial production growth accelerated to 10.1% yearon-year in November, from 9.6% in october, and was notably higher than the recent low of 8.9% recorded in august. also, the growth in fixed asset investment picked up to 20.7% in both october and November, from 20.2% in september, as policy-induced infrastructure investment began to ramp up. elsewhere, an improvement in consumer confidence over recent months contributed to an acceleration in retail sales growth to 14.9% in November, from a low of 13.1% in july. Finally, the chinese manufacturing Pmi rose to a 14-month high of 50.9 in December, from 50.5 in November, driven by a resurgence in domestic demand. ###### oecD leaDiNG iNDicaTor & Base meTals iNDeX ###### chiNese iP GroWTh & Base meTals iNDeX 105 Thomson Reuters GFMS 400

### ALUMINIUM ###### recent developments ###### outlook for the next twelve months **•** **_As the prospects for more quantitative easing grew, prices staged a rally through into early December. Increasing optimism over Chinese growth added to this upward trend, although more recently the US “fiscal cliff” and Eurozone worries have arrested any further rises. Recent additional QE announced by the Fed failed to spur another rally. Nevertheless, current aluminium prices are around 6% higher than at the end of 2011._** **•** **_The rally in markets seen through early December has

led us to revise higher our forecast for the fourth quarter average. We now expect this to be $2,000/tonne, and the 2012 average cash price to realise $2,018/tonne. The continued strength in global primary production, combined with the overall lacklustre demand environment, leads us to project market surpluses of 660,000 tonnes this year and 456,000 tonnes in 2013._** **•** **_LME stocks of aluminium registered yet another record high on November 29th, of 5.207 million tonnes. Vlissingen, in particular, has seen a notable net influx of metal. Aluminium inventories on the Shanghai Exchange also continued to build through November. The latest data for IAI unwrought stocks held by producers and aluminium held at major Japanese ports both showed declines in October. Total reported stocks have added 355,000 tonnes (5.2%) for the year-to-date._** **•** **_Whilst we continue to feel that monetary and fiscal stimulus will help to support markets going into 2013, the scope for any significant rallies, especially in the case of aluminium, remains limited. We are currently anticipating an average price of $2,125/tonne in the first quarter of next year and an annual average price in 2013 of $2,069/tonne._** **•** **_Following last month’s halt to the ongoing rise in physical premiums, this month saw European and Japanese quotes flatline, whilst US premiums eased slightly. Indications for first quarter Japanese term contracts are indicated in a lower range than for Q4. However, reports for premiums discussed for 2013 generally do not show any signs of any sharp turnaround._** **•** **_The global primary production rate remained steady in October, supported by ongoing robust Chinese output. Demand, meanwhile, continues to be driven by China and the United States, although Europe and now Japan are acting as a drag on consumption growth._** ###### thomson reuters Gfms’ forecast scenarIos **base case, 45% Probability** represents what thomson reuters Gfms consider the most likely outcome for the markets. **Scenario b, 40% Probability** faster recovery than under our base case in the near term and stronger growth thereafter. **Scenario c, 15% Probability** the crisis in the eurozone spreads to cause a markedly slower recovery in the mature economies and a moderation in chinese growth. ###### alumInIum supply-demand balance and prIce forecast ###### Quarterly alumInIum prIce forecast |(000 tonnes)
